analysis.one_liner: Raises Social Security benefits and pays for it with taxes on income above $250,000 and investment gains.
analysis.headline: The Social Security Expansion Act, backed by 42 House Democrats, has sat in three House committees without a hearing or vote since its February 2025 introduction.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would increase Social Security checks in several ways: a roughly 5-13% boost to benefit calculations, a cost-of-living formula tuned to what seniors actually buy, a new minimum benefit pegged to the poverty line for long-career low earners, and extended benefits for students whose parent was disabled or deceased. To pay for it and keep the program solvent, it would apply Social Security payroll taxes to all wages above $250,000 (currently wages are only taxed up to $176,100), quadruple-plus the tax on investment income, and merge the program's two trust funds.
analysis.who_benefits: Current and future Social Security retirees and disability beneficiaries get higher monthly checks through richer benefit formulas and a senior-specific inflation index. Lifetime low earners get a new minimum benefit of up to 125% of the poverty line if they worked 30 or more years. Full-time students who are the children of disabled or deceased workers can collect benefits until age 22 instead of losing them at 19. The tax changes are designed to make the program solvent long-term.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Retirees, disabled workers, and low earners

how_it_helps.text: Raises the first benefit 'bend point' from 90% to 95% and increases the second bend point by 18%, boosting monthly benefits for current and future beneficiaries.
Switches cost-of-living adjustments to the Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers, which tracks the spending patterns of people over 62.
Creates a new minimum benefit for long-career low earners, scaling from 6.25% of the poverty line at 11 years of work up to 125% at 30 or more years.
Lets full-time students who are children of disabled or deceased workers collect benefits until age 22, including under the Railroad Retirement Act.
Applies Social Security payroll taxes to wages and self-employment income above $250,000, raising revenue from the top slice of earners to fund benefits and solvency.
Raises the net investment income tax from 3.8% to 16.2% and extends it to active business income, dedicating 62% of that revenue to the Social Security Trust Fund.
Merges the Old-Age and Survivors and Disability trust funds into a single Social Security Trust Fund.

analysis.who_pays: High earners: anyone with wages or self-employment income above $250,000 would pay Social Security tax on the amount above that threshold, on top of what is taxed now. Wealthy investors and owners of pass-through businesses would pay a much higher tax on investment and business income (16.2% instead of 3.8%, now covering active business income). Employers of high earners would also pay the matching payroll tax above the threshold.
analysis.who_pays_short: High earners, investors, and business owners

drawbacks.text: The tax on net investment income would jump from 3.8% to 16.2% and would newly cover active trade or business income, a steep increase on investors and owners of pass-through businesses such as partnerships and S corporations.

Social Security payroll taxes would apply to all wages above $250,000 rather than stopping at the annual cap ($176,100 in 2025), raising combined payroll tax bills for high earners and their employers.

The benefit increases are large and apply to current beneficiaries immediately through recomputation, so the program's long-term balance depends entirely on the new taxes performing as projected; no independent cost estimate appears in the legislative record.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit side is broad and immediate: bigger checks for nearly all beneficiaries, a poverty-line floor for career low earners, and longer support for students of disabled or deceased parents. The cost side is a substantial, concentrated tax increase on income above $250,000 and on investment returns, including a quadrupled-plus investment income tax that some economists would argue discourages investment or pushes business income toward other forms. Whether the package is actuarially sound cannot be verified from the record, since no cost estimate has been produced. The design deliberately pairs expanded benefits with dedicated revenue, which is the main argument that it is fiscally responsible rather than a pure expansion.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in late February 2025 and referred to three House committees — Ways and Means plus Education and Workforce and Transportation and Infrastructure — none of which has scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Val Hoyle (D-OR) introduced the Social Security Expansion Act on February 27, 2025, joined by 19 original cosponsors, all Democrats.

The bill was referred to the Committees on Ways and Means, Education and Workforce, and Transportation and Infrastructure, with a portion also sent to the Railroads subcommittee; no further action has been taken since.
The bill has 41 cosponsors, all Democrats, and no Republican support in the record.

The bill would raise benefits for Social Security recipients, create a new minimum benefit pegged to the poverty line, extend student benefits to age 22, and fund the expansion with payroll taxes on income above $250,000 and a higher tax on investment income.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one's taxes have changed and no benefits have been raised. High earners and investors who would have paid the new taxes are better off for now; would-be beneficiaries have gained nothing because the bill has not advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High-income taxpayers who would have paid

for.name: Rep. Val Hoyle (D-OR)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Social Security Expansion Act and recruited 19 original Democratic cosponsors on the day of introduction.

for.name: 41 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, all from the Democratic caucus; none are Republicans.

against.name: Rep. Jason Smith (R-MO)
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the primary committee of referral, has not scheduled a markup or vote on the bill since its February 2025 referral.

sides.party_line_note: All 42 sponsors and cosponsors are Democrats; no Republican has signed on, and the bill has received no action in the Republican-controlled House.

industries.note: Would pay Social Security payroll tax on all wages above $250,000 instead of only on wages up to $176,100. That revenue funds the benefit increases and solvency fix for tens of millions of beneficiaries.
The net investment income tax would rise from 3.8% to 16.2%, with 62% of the revenue dedicated to the Social Security Trust Fund. This is the bill's largest new tax on concentrated wealth.

Active trade or business income would newly count as net investment income, subjecting many partnership and S-corporation owners to the higher 16.2% tax. Self-employed high earners would also pay Social Security tax on earnings above $250,000.

industries.industry: Social Security and railroad retirement beneficiaries
industries.note: Retirees, disabled workers, survivors, and student children of disabled or deceased workers would all receive richer or longer-lasting benefits, funded by the new taxes above.

analysis.trajectory: With a Republican House majority, zero Republican cosponsors, and no hearing or markup scheduled in any of the three committees months after referral, the bill is very unlikely to advance this Congress. Comparable Social Security expansion bills in prior Congresses also died in committee without a vote.
